articles.author: Howard Bryant
paras: A decade after Kaepernick’s quiet protest shook the NFL, his exile looks less like an aberration than a blueprint for the culture war that followed

America likes nice round numbers, perfect for anniversaries and reflections, and it has, suddenly, been 10 years since Colin Kaepernick first protested police killings – more accurately, police killings of Black people that went unpunished either internally or by the courts – by taking a knee during the national anthem for the entirety of the 2016 NFL regular season. He never played in the league again.

Ten years covers a lot of ground, especially in these years of American darkness, and many of the important details surrounding Kaepernick, his banishment and significance have disappeared, time replaced by more time and more darkness – time moving faster than ever, at internet speed, where nothing matters, where nothing sticks. We consume by clip, by click, by meme, and knowledge by meme is not knowledge at all.

articles.title: ‘Led us down such a dark path’: documentary explores how 9/11 changed America
articles.author: David Smith in Washington
paras: In Netflix film Turning Point: Generation 9/11, the lives of people forever impacted by the terrorist attack in 2001 are explored

Twenty-five years on, memory is giving way to history. Soon the US will cross the point where half its population were born after 11 September 2001 or were too young to remember the day that terrorists crashed planes into the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon in northern Virginia and a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

“When I do that math, I get to the bomb at Hiroshima – that’s how distant it is,” says Brian Knappenberger, 56, director of a new Netflix documentary, Turning Point: Generation 9/11 . “When we talk about the second world war, for our generation it seemed like a long time ago but, for the current generation of 20-year-olds, that’s how long ago it was.”

articles.title: White House ballroom cleared for now, but question remains: Can president legally use donations to build it?
articles.author:
<name>Ellen P. Aprill, Senior Scholar in Residence at the Lowell Milken Center for Philanthropy and Nonprofit Law, University of California, Los Angeles</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/ellen-p-aprill-526617"/>
paras: The fate of President Donald Trump’s estimated US$400 million White House ballroom may hinge on the little-known and somewhat surprising rules as to when the federal government and its agencies can accept privately donated funds.
That’s because Trump’s using the fact that he’s been accepting private donations to pay for at least some of the project’s cost as a justification for not needing Congress’ explicit authorization.

While a federal appeals court on Aug. 7, 2026, disagreed with the Trump administration, the Supreme Court on Aug. 31 said construction could go on . The 5-4 majority found that the preservationists who brought the case lacked standing, or legal grounds, to bring it in the first place because they were not directly harmed by the ballroom project. The majority did not address the underlying legal issues, which may or may not be resolved at a later date.

As a scholar of nonprofit and tax-exempt law who has studied for decades how the law governs deductible charitable contributions, including those to the government , I find that this case calls for an explanation of the role that such private donations may play in any federal government project or activity. An intricate statutory dance is required for taxpayers to make donations to particular government agencies or for particular government purposes.

You may not realize that you can make potentially tax-deductible contributions to the federal government itself. An official website lists almost two dozen programs , including the National Endowment for the Humanities, the National Arboretum and AmeriCorps, to which United States citizens can donate.

But such donations to government agencies are allowed only if Congress has granted the agency statutory authority to receive those funds. Moreover, authorized private donations are treated as if they have been appropriated by Congress .
The federal government has accepted donations voluntarily made by Americans since its founding .

What’s more, the Bureau of Fiscal Services – the central bank account and financial manager for the federal government – explains that it “may accept gifts donated to the United States Government” and that the account for such gifts, which dates back to 1843, was established “to accept gifts, such as bequests, from individuals wishing to express their patriotism to the United States.” Such gifts, however, are subject to restrictions.

In this context, according to the reasoning of the majority in the appeals court case, that means spending donated funds to preserve the existing East Wing would have been automatically allowed because it stood on a national park , and the National Park Service is an agency to which individuals can donate ; spending those funds to build something new to replace that structure would not be allowed unless Congress had authorized the project.
But the Trump administration has failed so far to obtain the needed congressional authorization and appropriations for the ballroom.

Since 1982, a provision of the United States Code, the official codification of all the nation’s general and permanent federal statutes, has required that these “patriotic” donations be devoted exclusively to reducing the national debt .

By law, federal agencies cannot augment congressional appropriations. The Miscellaneous Receipts Act requires that “an official or agent of the Government receiving money for the Government from any source shall deposit the money in the Treasury as soon as practicable without deduction for any charge or claim.”
Despite this seemingly absolute language, government agencies are permitted to accept gifts of money or other property when – and to the extent – they are given explicit statutory authority .
Agencies with the authority to accept gifts include the Justice Department, the State Department and the Library of Congress.

But any money, including donated funds, must be spent only as Congress directed in establishing the agency mission. The mission of the National Park Service is the conservation and preservation of the land and structures under its jurisdiction.
In contrast, the White House does not have this authority. Its own website states that it “is unable to accept cash, checks, bonds … or other monetary equivalents” as gifts from private citizens.
That’s in part why the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit held on Aug. 7 that Trump could not build the ballroom on the site of the former East Wing building .

The two judges in the majority concluded that neither the National Park Service, which is the steward for the national park on which the White House stands, nor Trump himself had satisfied all the statutory requirements needed to undertake building of the above-ground ballroom. It did not block work on an underground military bunker the Trump administration began renovating after it demolished the East Wing in October 2025 .

That some, most or even all the funding comes from private donations does not protect the administration’s right to proceed with construction of the 90,000-square-foot (8,361-square-meter) ballroom because it has failed so far to obtain congressional authorization and appropriations for this project, the majority explained.

Crucial to this conclusion was a statute declaring, “A building or structure shall not be erected on any reservation, park, or public grounds of the Federal Government in the District of Columbia without express authority of Congress.”

“We are aware of no instance in American history in which a President unilaterally and using privately collected funds demolished substantial portions of the White House that Congress authorized to be built and American taxpayers paid for,” the majority opinion says. “Until now.”

The four dissenting justices in the Aug. 31 Supreme Court decision seemed to agree that there is “ an apparent absence of statutory authority ” for the project, noting that Congress must expressly approve the construction of any “building or structure” on any federal park in the District of Columbia.
The Trump administration has pointed to two possible statutes it says provides the necessary authority to build the ballroom.

One involves the purposes for which the National Park Service can spend its funds, including privately donated funds. The other grants the president the ability to spend funds for, among other items, “the care, maintenance, repair, alteration, refurnishing, [and] improvement” of the executive residence at the White House – funds that “are authorized to be appropriated each fiscal year.”
The majority in the appeals court decision explained that authority for the president to construct the ballroom requires satisfying both of those statutes; neither alone suffices.

And it rejected the reliance on the National Park Service provision alone. That statute limits use of the service’s funds, in the words of the majority, to “the identified purposes of conservation and preservation.”

In particular, the majority ruled, the provision does not authorize the construction of a new building. Further, it held, the National Park Service provision cannot authorize the president to lead the project; only the provision related to the executive residence can do that.
As to the executive residence provision, the majority opinion explains that it “does not expressly grant the President any independent authority.”
Instead, the majority held, the president must rely on “an accompanying appropriation.” The court found no such accompanying appropriation.

The Supreme Court majority, in its decision, did not address the merits of the argument. So even as the case continues, the ruling means opponents of the ballroom project will need to find someone who’s suffered actual harm in order to overcome this hurdle.
This is an updated version of an article originally published on Aug. 20, 2026.

Ellen P. Aprill does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: How students at Colorado State helped teach their community to stop talking past each other and manage complex problems
articles.author:
<name>Martin Carcasson, Director, Center for Public Deliberation, Colorado State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/martin-carcasson-317599"/>
paras: On a Thursday evening in Fort Collins, Colorado, community members gathered around tables to discuss whether the city should allow marijuana dispensaries within city limits.

Rather than take turns for two minutes at a microphone, the participants considered various viewpoints, engaged with quality information and focused on exploring solutions that worked to mitigate the concerns of the critics but still supported the goals of the advocates.

Gatherings like this one have happened more than 500 times in and around the northern Colorado town over the past 20 years. Each was facilitated by college students. While outrage and polarization dominate many political discussions , these events provide compelling evidence that when offered a more nuanced way of engaging, the public recognizes the value and calls for more.

I’m a communication studies professor with a background in argumentation and debate. I founded the Colorado State University Center for Public Deliberation in 2006 based on the theory that democracy requires high-quality communication and engagement to thrive . Existing political, journalistic and social media systems rarely provide such opportunities, but a growing number of organizations like the center are learning more about how to provide them.
Initially, my research centered on national politics. As I learned how issues like poverty , race and the environment were discussed, I became frustrated.

I came to understand that social issues are best understood as “wicked problems ” that involve competing underlying values that are inherently in tension with each other . These tensions stand in the way of “solving” the problem long term. In a diverse society where people reasonably prioritize values differently, it is clear that addressing wicked problems requires a more collaborative style of communication .
Research in social psychology and brain science, however, shows humans are simply not wired for these conversations.

Scholarship reveals that humans are motivated reasoners susceptible to numerous unconscious biases that undermine their ability to engage complex issues. Humans are prone to confirmation bias and my-side bias , so we tend to cherry-pick the facts that support our preconceived ideas and reject those that challenge them. We often suffer from an inflated sense of certainty .

Humans are also narrative creatures who prefer simple stories with clear heroes, victims and villains. We have a natural attraction to divisive, identity-based appeals that too often see the world through us-them frames that lead to divisiveness and contempt .
In other words, when given a choice, humans strongly prefer to assume that problems are caused by wicked people, rather that engage the inherent wickedness of problems.

By the end of graduate school, I understood that a highly partisan two-party system makes a problematic situation worse by rewarding the exploitation of these human tendencies. As a result, adversarial politics lead to an exaggerated sense of polarization that breeds divisiveness and misunderstanding. They can also fuel information chaos , an overwhelming swirl of misinformation and disinformation that the researchers with RAND aptly named Truth Decay . Information chaos is also directly related to the erosion of trust in journalism and academia , two institutions that traditionally helped elevate quality information.

This adversarial environment is also a ripe breeding ground for bad faith actors who undermine our civic culture. There is a growing recognition among civic engagement scholars and practitioners that conflict profiteers , merchants of doubt and polarizers actively work to take advantage of human biases for their own benefit.

Above all, I recognized that how people engage each other matters . I decided to explore alternative models of engagement better suited to how our brains worked as well as the problems our communities were facing.

The practice of deliberation is a form of structured interactive communication designed to help people engage with complex issues and come to more reasoned judgments. I began experimenting with this new tool in my classroom starting in around 2000. At first I adopted material from the National Issues Forums Institute , a nonpartisan organization that has been developing deliberative discussion guides for educational purposes since 1981.
I was hired at Colorado State University in 2003 to take over the argumentation and debate class, and I shifted the class’s focus from debate to deliberation.

The course challenged students to frame an issue from a deliberative perspective by asking, “What should we do about X?” with X being a shared wicked problem, such as the increasing number of mental health issues on campus.

The assignment shifted students from being advocates of a particular viewpoint to serving as impartial analysts. Many assignments in K-12 and college education ask students to start with a conclusion and then do research to support it, encouraging motivated reasoning. This assignment was designed to force their brains to see different sides of an issue by adopting what author Julia Galef describes as a “ scout mindset .”

Students developed a well-researched discussion guide that outlined at least three distinct approaches to address their problem. These guides served as useful tools for others to overcome my-side bias and exaggerated polarization and to be more likely to, as psychologist Adam Grant has encouraged, think again .
In 2006, the Center for Public Deliberation launched.

To support it, I designed a course that trains students to facilitate small-group discussions. Our first major project involved running six nights of forums for the local school district that engaged over 600 participants in a discussion about reorganizing schools. My students and I worked with them to and successfully debuted a deliberative form of engagement.

Soon we were designing and running events for the city, county, university and community organizations on issues such as housing affordability and decarbonization. College students facilitated every event.

Our work shows that the events our student facilitators supported had a positive impact on the quality of local engagement. Well-designed and well-facilitated processes bring out the best of human nature, particularly our creativity , cooperative social instincts and sense of purpose . They can rebuild trust and provide hope for democracy .

Since 2006, our staff has grown. The center has continued to refine our methods, drawing from the interdisciplinary academic field of deliberative democracy and using resources from practitioner organizations focused on quality engagement and collaboration, such as the National Coalition for Dialogue and Deliberation , the Interactivity Foundation and the International Association for Public Participation .

Similar centers for civic life have developed on other campuses. The Center for Public Deliberation is currently a part of a Department of Education grant to further expand the network to 40 campuses across the country.

Beyond campus, organizations such as Braver Angels , Better Together America and the Trust for Civic Life are dedicated to building local civic hubs that use these tools. They also train facilitators and serve as critical bridging institutions between diverse groups.

The challenges our communities face are significant. But every day more people are realizing that how we engage each other matters and are making space for the conversations that must be sparked for democracy to thrive.
Read more of our stories about Colorado .

Martin Carcasson works for the Colorado State University Center for Public Deliberation, serves as the co-chair of the Braver Angels Civic Scholars Council, and partners with organizations such at National Issues Forum, the Interactivty Foundation, and the National Coalition for Dialogue and Deliberation.

articles.title: Data center projects in Pennsylvania face stronger local scrutiny after Shapiro’s executive order
articles.author:
<name>Michael Helbing, Adjunct Professor of Law, Penn State</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/michael-helbing-2673295"/>
paras: Governors across the country are relying on their executive powers to address the increasing public backlash against data center proposals.

In July 2026, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul placed an effective moratorium on data center permitting until the state’s Department of Public Service creates a generic environmental impact statement regarding the impacts of data centers. Similarly, in August 2026, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott announced a moratorium on data centers until state agencies can audit data related to impacts on the electric grid.
In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro signed executive order 2026-05 on Aug. 18, 2026, placing restrictions on the state’s review of permits related to data centers.

I am the executive director of Penn State’s Center for Energy Law and Policy , and I have been tracking policy responses to data center proposals in Pennsylvania and across the country. I find it notable that one of the justifications the governor appears to cite in his order is a little-used but potentially powerful legal tool: the Environmental Rights Amendment to the Pennsylvania Constitution .

Shapiro’s executive order does not completely stop data center permitting activities. But it does add requirements that may slow their development and give local officials more influence over the process:
The order makes all data center projects ineligible for the PA Permit Fast Track Program , which streamlines permitting for certain high-impact projects.
It prohibits any agencies under the governor’s oversight from entering into nondisclosure agreements in connection with a data center project.
It requires the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection to create a public map that shows permitting information about all known data center projects in the state.

Perhaps most significantly, it prohibits officials from issuing state permits for data center projects until after the developer has demonstrated it has complied with local plans and received all required municipal approvals. This ordering of permitting has the potential to enhance local power over data center projects.

The order also creates a two-tiered system for permitting review. One tier is for developers that agree to comply with the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development, or GRID, standards . The other is for developers that do not comply.

Among other things, the GRID standards call for developers to secure all energy needed to power their facility, including a portion powered by clean energy; pay 100% of the costs of their project; and comply with environmental operating and reporting requirements.

Developers that agree to comply with the GRID standards will have their state permit applications reviewed on a rolling basis when they are submitted and issued on a rolling basis after all local requirements are met.

For projects that do not comply with the GRID standards, the state’s Department of Environmental Protection will not even begin reviewing state permit applications until the developers have obtained all necessary local permits.

Collectively, the policies in the executive order are likely to both slow down the permitting process for data centers and give local officials more leverage over data center projects. Municipal officials have significant authority over local land use decisions. Now that state permit review is contingent on local approvals, data center developers will have more incentive to work with local decision-makers to minimize delays.
Beyond the scope of the order itself, I find it significant that the executive order cites “Pennsylvanians’ constitutional rights” as part of its justification.
Although the order does not specify which constitutional rights it is referring to, it appears to be a reference to the Pennsylvania Constitution’s Environmental Rights Amendment .

The Environmental Rights Amendment is in Article 1 of the Pennsylvania Constitution , along with political rights such as the freedom of speech and freedom of religion. It guarantees the people’s “right to clean air, pure water, and to the preservation of the natural, scenic, historic and esthetic values of the environment.”

Although it was added to the state Constitution in 1971 , the impact of the Environmental Rights Amendment has been muted until recently. Earlier court decisions limited the legal power of the amendment. But recent opinions from the Pennsylvania Supreme Court have given it new life , raising legal questions about how the amendment will be interpreted in the future. Those cases clarified that it is not necessarily enough for the state to simply comply with environmental statutes. A law or state action that “ unreasonably impairs ” the right to clean air, pure water or other environmental values can be deemed unconstitutional.

If the commonwealth cites the Environmental Rights Amendment in litigation defending the executive order on data centers, courts will have another opportunity to interpret the amendment’s language – and therefore its power. Judges will be called upon to weigh how Pennsylvania’s constitutional obligations to protect its citzens’ rights to a clean environment are properly balanced against industry’s procedural and property rights to develop land. Depending on how courts decide those cases, the commonwealth – and even citizens – may have a more robust weapon in their fight for “clean air, pure water, and to the preservation of the natural, scenic, historic and esthetic values of the environment” going forward.

articles.title: The greenest building is the one still standing after a disaster
articles.author:
<name>Fernanda Cruz Rios, Assistant Professor of Civil, Architectural and Environmental Engineering, Drexel University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/fernanda-cruz-rios-2749515"/>
paras: When Hurricane Michael tore through the Florida Panhandle in 2018, a beach house called the Sand Palace was left standing , while more than half the buildings around it were destroyed.

Its owners had built it to withstand roughly double the wind speed that Florida’s code required, with reinforced concrete walls on 40-foot (12-meter) pilings. The cost was about 15% to 20% more than standard construction , but the owners wanted a house that could survive storms.

Designers usually measure how “green” a building is by its carbon footprint – the greenhouse gases released making, transporting and running everything that goes into it. The Sand Palace’s extra concrete expanded its carbon footprint, making the house appear less environmentally friendly on paper.

But a green building has to last for its intentionally small carbon footprint to make a positive difference. Damage from a flood, a wildfire or a hurricane can require significantly more building materials to repair it, ballooning its carbon footprint over time .

As storms happen more often and with more intensity, considering the full life cycle of a building and its costs over time becomes increasingly important to get an accurate picture of how sustainable that building really is.
Insurers may be the biggest force getting builders to consider durability .

Building codes are only beginning to take climate change into account. And green ratings like LEED – which encourage builders to make sustainable choices in exchange for the cache of the rating, which can increase property value – assess new buildings when they’re built, not after they’ve been battered by storms.

Insurers, however, have more incentive to look at the long-term costs . They often offer discounts of 15% to 30% off hurricane coverage for fortifying homes because they price a building’s risk over the life of a policy instead of just its condition on Day 1. For builders, that can mean building or retrofitting with reinforced roofing, impact-resistant windows and similar upgrades that meet independently verified wind standards.
Studies that measure how much damage could be avoided from resilient design have found a similar payoff.

For example, a study of flood-prevention infrastructure in coastal Catalonia, Spain, found that flood barriers and channel improvements generated more greenhouse gas emissions during construction, but they prevented an estimated 58 metric tons of carbon-equivalent emissions per flood. Within 25 years, the emissions avoided from damage were expected to balance out the emissions from the improvements, well inside the infrastructure’s 50-year expected lifespan. Financially, the payback was far faster: about two years.
The next step is expanding that logic into standards that already shape most construction decisions.

Researchers, including myself, are proposing ways to bring resilience into the equation . Accounting for the materials, energy and disruption to a building during and after a disaster would show the true costs of a building that’s too damaged to function.
Three pieces are missing from that equation right now:

The first is the cost of keeping people and operations running while a damaged building is out of commission: temporary shelter, emergency generators, transportation for evacuated residents or relocated staff. None of that currently counts toward a building’s environmental footprint even though it’s a direct consequence of how that building was designed.

The second is the cost of adapting a building after an event – not just repairing it, but upgrading it to withstand the next one. That might include reinforcing a foundation that failed, elevating utilities that flooded, or replacing what was there with something built to survive next time. Each carries environmental costs that current assessments don’t measure.

The third is recognizing the damage, repairs and downtime that a resilient design choice helps a building’s owners and tenants avoid altogether. Examples already exist, like the coastal infrastructure case in Spain . What’s missing is automatically including these benefits into green-building and infrastructure assessments.

Together, these show up as real costs – in dollars, in carbon emissions and in the lives disrupted when a hospital or home loses functionality for months instead of days. They’re costs that insurers, the designers of building codes and ratings systems all have a reason to shrink.

We already know how to build homes like the Sand Palace that can stand up to disasters. What’s missing isn’t the engineering; it’s incentive to build for durability as the rule rather than the exception.

Dr. Fernanda Cruz Rios's research lab has received funding from the National Science Foundation, the Lemelson Foundation, the American Society for Engineering Education, and the Pennsylvania Department of Community and Economic Development.

articles.title: What is public interest technology? An expert on data and policy explains how it helps people in need
articles.author:
<name>Rayid Ghani, Distinguished Career Professor of Machine Learning and Public Policy, Carnegie Mellon University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/rayid-ghani-2735787"/>
paras: Every year, millions of people who qualify for food assistance never get it. The money exists and they meet the eligibility rules, but they don’t know that the program exists, or if they qualify. For others, the application is too long and complicated.
Public interest technology can fill these gaps between what a policy promises and what a person experiences.

Public interest technology is a combination of technology, data, design, policy, social science, ethics and law brought together to improve people’s lives and serve the common good. Public interest technology has prevented children from being poisoned by lead paint , helped families stay in their homes instead of being evicted, and supported disaster recovery efforts after the Los Angeles fires .
The work is carried out by government agencies, nonprofit organizations, universities, community groups and experts like me who study how to use technology to help solve societal issues.
Public interest technology starts with identifying the problem and asking two questions: What system is not working for the people it is supposed to serve? And how can it be improved?

The next step involves building a cross-disciplinary team to address the situation and scoping the problem. A caseworker, for example, knows things that no analyst can discover from data. A community member knows the reality on the ground. Data scientists, designers, engineers and policy experts, as well as the people affected, create the technology together.

Once there is an initial design for a solution, the team iteratively develops the system, validates that it functions as intended, evaluates whether its impact is equitable, and field-tests it to reveal errors and measure impact.

Impact is the bottom line. A pilot program that ends in an academic paper or a press release does not help people. Impact means the system works, the community trusts it and uses it, and people’s lives improve.

Chicago used to wait until a child’s blood test came back positive for lead before inspecting a home for lead sources. That sequence protects the next child who will live there, but not the current one. A data-driven system that we helped develop tracks housing stock, building permits and health information in order to flag high-risk housing units, allowing the health department to conduct preventive inspections before a child gets poisoned.

Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, has a limited budget to help the 10,000 to 15,000 people who receive eviction notices each year. A machine learning system now identifies the residents most likely to become homeless, so the county’s limited outreach efforts and scarce dollars reach the people who need help the most.

Johnson County, Kansas, linked its jail system, emergency medical service and mental health service so it could identify people cycling between crisis and incarceration. The system helps mental health workers identify and reach out to people at risk before the next arrest.

Some cities are expanding public interest technology in-house. New York just launched the Public Interest Technology Crew , which embeds technology specialists in agencies to solve problems for residents. The first crew, embedded in the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, is building a portal for New Yorkers to report violations of click-to-cancel subscription laws .

Organizations such as the U.S. Digital Corps , Coding it Forward and Data Science for Social Good (which I co-founded) are creating partnerships between technology specialists and employees in governments and nonprofits. And universities are starting to weave public interest technology into curricula, largely driven by the Public Interest Technology University Network , a consortium of universities, cities and foundations.

What makes a technology a public interest technology is a set of choices: who helps build it, how its success is defined, and who is accountable when it gets things wrong. Made correctly, those choices mean the person who qualifies for food assistance isn’t left waiting for it.

articles.title: Many space missions are searching for life beyond Earth – but are we prepared for the fallout if they succeed?
articles.author:
<name>Margaret E. Kosal, Associate Professor of International Affairs, Georgia Institute of Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/margaret-e-kosal-2280532"/>
paras: Microbes from space have fueled the plots of science fiction mainstays like “ Project Hail Mary ” and “ The Andromeda Strain .” But with more space missions launching each year, finding extraterrestrial life in a microbial form is becoming more plausible. What will the response be back here on Earth if – or when – scientists discover extraterrestrial microbes? Will the international policy and security communities be prepared for the fallout?

When you hear about extraterrestrial life, your mind may go to intelligent life, like the kind present in a lot of Hollywood science fiction. But even the confirmation of microbial life that originated somewhere other than on Earth – which is much more likely – would be a paradigm-shifting event. Thinking about what these consequences might look like early on can help nations and the international community prepare.

Our team is interested in this question. We’re made up of a full professor of international affairs, who earned a Ph.D. in chemistry, and whose expertise is on how emerging science and technologies could affect global conflict and cooperation, as well as an emerging scholar in space policy and security and an expert on social and political implications of frontier technologies, such as AI, space, quantum and energy sources.

Multiple Mars landers have identified large amounts of frozen and liquid water , essential for life, on the red planet. Samples retrieved by Japan’s Hayabusa2 spacecraft from a near-Earth asteroid revealed the presence of uracil , part of RNA, which is a building block of life. Uncrewed space probes like NASA’s Europa Clipper and the European Space Agency’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer are on their way to conduct detailed reconnaissance of the planet’s moons and to investigate whether they have conditions suitable for life.

Along with data from the James Webb Space Telescope and future missions targeting Saturn’s icy moon Enceladus , the likelihood of discovering extraterrestrial microbial life has increased substantially.
The discovery of microbial life would expose significant gaps in international governance related to space.

While there are some existing international agreements, including the Outer Space Treaty , that provide space law guidelines, these are ill-equipped to address the complexities posed by extraterrestrial biology.

The Outer Space Treaty , established in 1967, dictates that countries should use outer space peacefully. It also states that no single nation may claim ownership or exert sovereignty over parts of outer space or celestial bodies such as the Moon.

However, it doesn’t have much to say about who can own extraterrestrial organisms or what to do about biosecurity risks. It doesn’t have direction for who can use, preserve or destroy living things, such as bacteria or fungi, that may be discovered in space.
While people have yet to discover extraterrestrial life of any kind, there are some major geopolitical events that can help researchers understand what the consequences might look like.

While the space race of the 1950s and ’60s led to exploration of the Moon, it was driven by a Cold War power struggle between two nations back on Earth. Instead of coming together to explore space, both countries experienced a renewed sense of nationalism . They used the new discoveries that came from the space race to invest in their military capabilities.

On the other hand, researchers can look at how states respond to asteroid threats . Since an asteroid could pose a truly existential threat from space, preventing the worst-case scenario requires cooperation and thinking ahead.

Astronomers have built a global, collaborative network to monitor for and sound the alarm about any potential threats. This network has shown that nations can put aside terrestrial rivalries to work together if they perceive something from space as a truly existential threat.

The International Space Station is another example showing how nations that are competing great powers on Earth work together to cooperate in space. Countries have collaborated to solve issues on the International Space Station that have specific, short-term and clearly identified goals.

These examples show a range of possible reactions to the discovery of space microbes. The situation could renew space races between competing countries and lead to militarization, or it could create unprecedented cooperation.
We’ve identified three main possible outcomes to the discovery of microbial extraterrestrial life.

First, there’s a cooperative outcome, reminiscent of the asteroid threat network or the International Space Station . Here, nations collaborate to regulate research, share data, protect the planet or advance specific interests they share.
This pathway isn’t inherently benign or malignant. It could entail expanding the roles of international organizations or creating new legal instruments .

Second there’s a competitive outcome, characterized by strategic rivalry between countries. Like in the space race, nations could fight to be technologically superior . They might try to monopolize access to the extraterrestrial microbes or to leverage biological discoveries from the microbes for their own economic or military advantage.

Scientific breakthroughs derived from extraterrestrial organisms could lead to innovations in medicine, agriculture, energy and beyond. However, the organisms could also be weaponized, intentionally or otherwise, which would amplify biosecurity risks . In this sense, the discovery of microbial life could create a new form of technological competition, one that merges space exploration with biological research and development.

The increasing role of private companies , such as SpaceX, complicates this dynamic. These companies receive contracts from the government, blurring the lines between commercial civilian and strategic activities.

For example, around 60% of all satellites currently orbiting the Earth belong to SpaceX’s Starlink subsidiary. The company can – and has – chosen to block access selectively, in alignment with its political priorities. When commercial interests and national priorities diverge, who has access versus who is denied access can be uncertain.

Research around biopiracy may come into play. Biopiracy is a term that applies to two primary issues: the patenting of indigenous knowledge or the patenting of natural resources, such as microbes, for profit. The Budapest Treaty prohibits claiming ownership of a naturally occurring microbe on Earth, but there’s no equivalent for microbes in space.

Third is an isolationist outcome, in which states could sever their involvement in international cooperation due to biosecurity concerns or political distrust. The potential for unknown biological risks, however minimal, could trigger precautionary restrictions on data sharing , which limits international collaboration.
Countries may lose or gain allies as they grapple with whether the microbe could cause harm to humans or the environment, or be developed into a biological weapon.

Emerging technologies will also shape these outcomes. Artificial intelligence and machine learning are already integral to scientific research. Scientists use them to process astronomical data and identify potential biosignatures . Nanotechnology and advances in the life sciences and engineering could allow researchers to study, modify or exploit extraterrestrial microbes, if they’re given access to them.

Countries will have to prepare not only for the scientific implications of discovery but also for its societal and political reverberations. The politicization of scientific discoveries from the microbes could complicate or change how countries respond domestically and at the international scale. Misinformation about the microbes could shape policy and public response .
The discovery of extraterrestrial microbial life would not merely mark a scientific milestone. It would be a geopolitical event.

Rather than attempting to predict a singular outcome, policymakers could adopt scenario-based planning approaches in the meantime to anticipate and prepare for a range of possibilities. In these approaches, participants explore multiple futures through structured activities similar to professional or military wargaming or path games , in which they explore multiple outcomes systematically to test strategies, to plan and to analyze potential outcomes under realistic uncertainty.
In our view, the question is not whether humanity will discover life beyond Earth, but whether it is prepared for the consequences when it does.

articles.title: Compass and Northwest Multiple Listing Service settle 16-month legal battle
articles.author: Lillian Dickerson
paras: This story originally appeared on Real Estate News .
Compass and the Washington state-based Northwest Multiple Listing Service (NWMLS) have settled their year-plus-long lawsuit, Compass announced on Monday.

Compass and NWMLS have agreed to a settlement through the creation of a new listing status that will allow Compass agents to pre-market their properties without risk of being fined by the MLS. The new status, which will become effective Sept. 4, is called “First Look” and will be treated similarly to a coming-soon listing, according to a press release.

When requested by the seller, the status allows showings for brokers and their clients, open houses and offers to be made on a property without incurring public price changes or days on market for up to 21 days while preparing for an “Active” status launch.

NWMLS clarified that days in the “First Look” status and any pre-launch price adjustments will be available internally to members of the NWMLS database but will not be published publicly. The MLS also said sellers can choose whether a “First Look” is published on IDX websites “or choose to engage in more tailored public marketing.”
Compass International Holdings Chairman and CEO Robert Reffkin said the brokerage’s goal in launching its lawsuit against NWMLS “has been fully realized.”

“We brought this lawsuit on a fundamental principle: homeowners deserve the absolute right to control how their properties are marketed, and real estate brokers should never face fines from NWMLS simply for following their client’s lawful instructions which in Washington State is their Statutory Duty,” Reffkin said in a statement.
Compass “proudly invested millions” in the lawsuit, Reffkin added, “and it was worth it.”

“MLSs are a group of direct competitors that are telling their competitors how they can and can not compete, which is the textbook definition of an antitrust violation,” Reffkin continued. “MLSs exist to distribute listings, when the homeseller wants to use it, not to let brokerage competitors collectively dictate how other brokers compete in marketing services or how homesellers market their homes.”
In a news release, NWMLS said the “First Look” status was created in response to member feedback — specifically amid shifting consumer expectations.

“We are giving sellers the flexibility they desire when preparing a home for market, while steadfastly protecting buyers from private networks,” NWMLS President and CEO Justin Haag said in a statement. “Simply put, First Look modernizes the pre-launch preparation process, while ensuring an open marketplace and fair competition, in full compliance with Washington State’s open-market laws.”

The MLS’s announcement also noted that the new status enables NWMLS to resolve litigation with Compass “while reaffirming its commitment to an open and comprehensive marketplace, data integrity, and consumer protection across the Pacific Northwest.”
In a blog post published on Monday, Redfin also praised NWMLS’s move to create the new listing status.

“This is exactly the kind of innovation sellers, agents and major industry players — including Redfin — have been calling for, and we salute NWMLS for pioneering a pro-consumer, pro-competition solution,” said the post authored by Joe Rath, head of industry relations at Redfin parent Rocket Companies.

Back in April, Rath authored a separate open letter published on the company’s website that implored NWMLS to change its pre-marketing policies, arguing in favor of “homeseller choice,” a phrase used often by Reffkin. Redfin and Compass partnered in February to allow the brokerage’s “Private Exclusive” and “Coming Soon” listings to be published on Redfin.
In his Monday post, Rath also reiterated an argument Redfin made earlier this year that providing sellers with more pre-marketing options could ultimately give for-sale inventory a boost .

Compass sued NWMLS last April, alleging that the MLS engaged in anticompetitive business practices, obstruction of seller choice and retaliation through a temporary suspension of Compass’ IDX feed . At the time, Compass claimed that it spent months trying to negotiate rule changes with NWMLS to allow for the brokerage’s office exclusives, but NWMLS “simply refused.”
Last June, NWMLS filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit , but a judge denied the motion in March 2026.

Then, in April of this year, NWMLS filed a counterclaim against Compass , alleging that the brokerage’s 3-phased marketing strategy violates the Washington Consumer Protection Act because it is a “deceptive scheme” designed to conceal data from the public at large. NWMLS also argued that its own MLS rules were reaffirmed through a new state law seeking to restrict private listings.
In addition to the new listing status, several other terms were agreed to as part of the settlement.

By Oct. 15, NWMLS has agreed to require all portals and real estate websites that use the MLS’s data to clearly and prominently display the name and contact information of real estate brokers on a listing, and immediately next to any contact broker buttons so that buyers have clear and direct access to the listing broker.
By that same date, NWMLS must also stop placing its watermarks on listing photographs to “[ensure] that NWMLS does not take credit for the work of real estate professionals.”

NWMLS is further obligated to apply its rules across all brokerages in the state of Washington to ensure they receive equal treatment, and it will be prohibited from taking legal action against Compass or its real estate professionals “under the guise of ‘enforcing state law,'” Compass said. The point references the new Washington state law that took effect in mid-June , which seeks to limit the use of private marketing practices in real estate. The language of the law, however, is vague, and therefore how much it may curb private listings in practice is uncertain.

By Nov. 15, NWMLS must also “give broker platforms the data fields and supplements that are relevant for brokers to do their jobs (eg, Legal, Firpta, 22k, 22j, Prelim, Surveys/maps, Resale cert), unless legally prohibited,” Compass said, so that brokers don’t have to access multiple systems to complete their work functions.

articles.title: Amazon accused of rigging ad auctions to inflate prices in new suit filed by FTC and 22 states
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Amazon is accused of artificially inflating the ad prices on its e-commerce site in a lawsuit filed Monday by Washington’s attorney general, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and 21 other states.
Amazon denies the allegations, saying its ad pricing has not harmed advertisers or shoppers and that the FTC’s claims mischaracterize how its system works.

Ads are sold on Amazon’s platform through so-called “second-price” auctions, in which businesses set a maximum price they’re willing to pay for an ad. If they’re the highest bidder, they pay only one cent more than the second-highest bid, and the auctions do not allow advertisers to see other bids.
Plaintiffs allege that beginning in late 2018, Amazon started adding surcharges to the prices, despite claims that it was still using a second-price system.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington in Seattle, alleges the tech giant overcharged roughly 1.2 million ad customers by overriding and replacing auction results with “higher prices set by Amazon to increase its profits.” The amount collected through the allegedly deceptive pricing scheme totals $20 billion, according to the suit.

“Many small business owners in Washington rely on Amazon for their livelihoods, and our office is committed to making sure Amazon treats them fairly, transparently, and in accordance with the law,” said Nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, in a statement.

Amazon posted an online response to the allegations. “The FTC’s claim fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate,” the company stated. “Advertisers adjust bids based on real-world performance, not descriptions of auction mechanics.”

The company said it prioritizes the relevance of an ad to the shoppers being targeted over bid price alone. As a result, Amazon said, 92% of winning ads in recent years were not given to the highest bidder, and ad performance has improved. Conversion rates — the percentage of shoppers who take a desired action after interacting with an ad — rose 24% from 2021 to 2025, according to Amazon.
The company also said that from 2019 to 2024, the average cost-per-click for sponsored product search ads was flat when adjusted for inflation.

Amazon acknowledged it has changed its ad pricing approach over time, saying that as the system prioritized ad relevance, winning bids increasingly fell below market value. As a result, the company now sets minimum prices, or “reserves,” for participating in an auction and for the minimum market value of the ad.
“Reserves like these,” it said, “are common across the industry.” The company said it does not charge advertisers more than their bid.
Amazon said it clearly explains its pricing process to advertisers. Plaintiffs dispute that, citing company employees who described creating fake auction participants.

The suit states that an Amazon senior scientist said that to increase auction prices, the company inserts “an invented auction participant representing how much Amazon thinks that particular ad slot is worth.”

The lawsuit is being led by the FTC and also includes the attorneys general of Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina and Vermont.
The company is also in the FTC’s crosshairs in a separate, broader antitrust case accusing Amazon of maintaining an illegal monopoly in online retail, which is scheduled for trial next year.
Plaintiffs in the case announced Monday are asking the court to order Amazon to reform its practices, pay restitution and civil penalties for each violation, and cover attorneys’ fees.

articles.title: Link Ends Earlier, Starts Later
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: Several comments have raised concerns that the August 29th service change shortened Link’s service day, so that it now ends earlier and starts later. This interacts with the launch of ST Express “Night Ride” routes between midnight and 4am. These theoretically can replace Link trips. But the ST Express routes bypass several high-ridership Seattle Link stations. This can force trips that were on Link in the midnight hour or 11 pm hour or 4 am hour to an ST Express or Metro route, turn a 1-seat ride into a 2-seat ride, and the bus routes are less frequent than Link was.

I wanted to know, did the spans really change on August 29? What is the current situation on weekdays, Saturdays, and Sundays? What kinds of trips at what hours are newly 2-seat rides? Where is the best place to live to have the earliest or latest Link service? Which can you go to on those lucky runs?

I looked at the new 1 Line and 2 Line schedules to quantify the current situation and changes. To reach these pages from Sound Transit’s website, use the schedule form on the home page to get to the interactive charts. To get a PDF of the schedule, go to the bottom of the page and press the “Full Schedule PDF” button.
I tried to make a consolidated list that would organize the first/last runs in different areas and days. But it was an insanely difficult job, and after a few hours I gave up.
So instead we’re going to crowdsource the issue.

How has Link’s span changed since August 29th? Has this affected your trips? Or do you see other people’s trips that are affected? Can you glean more from the schedules than I can? Can you figure out the right questions to ask AI to figure it out? (If you do, please disclose AI’s role in the result.)

Some of these impacts have already come up in recent articles’ comments, but this article is a place to consolidate them all together so we can see the total impact. And it will be a reference in the future when people have a question, so that they can find it all in one easy-to-find place.

The problem I had with the interactive schedule pages was I had to keep scrolling four directions to get at the first or last full run and short run, and when that would get you to Westlake or SeaTac or the final terminus. I had to keep going up to the date switcher. I kept finding mistake after mistake in my results, so I had to go back and reconfirm them, or compare weekday to Saturday again, and make sure I hadn’t jumped back to a date before the service change. Reading the PDFs online was a lot of up-and-down scrolling with similar printing. Printing the PDFs to get a wider-area view at once would take 34 pages per line. Maybe ST has a printed schedule book with them but I’d have to go search for a copy. I didn’t want to publish a list with mistakes that would waste everybody’s time.
Maybe if different people address small parts of the issue individually, we can get those facts more accurately and a better idea of the whole.

ST in the future wants to shorten Link’s span further, or have more single-track reductions, or more weekend closures of segments, to increase the time available for maintenance. We desperately want ST to increase maintenance because Link’s reliability is far below peer cities’ networks. This causes passengers to get stuck en route, be late for appointments, or drive to critical appointments to avoid the risk that Link will hiccup that day. It also snares visitors and gives them a negative impression of Seattle and Seattle’s transit. So we really want maintenance to be increased to make Link more reliable.

At the same time we need Link’s late-night and early-morning service. If ST Express night owls bypass several Seattle stations in the shoulder hours Link used to provide, then it’s not an adequate substitute. ST says Metro has night owl buses in all those areas (7, 36, 49, 67, 70). But those night runs are funded by Seattle’s transit levy, and will go away if voters don’t renew the levy this November. Metro stopped funding Seattle night owls in the 2014 recession. Also, the bus routes are half-hourly or hourly, as opposed to Link’s 15 minutes. If you switch to say the 49+597 or 36+597 to workaround the loss of Link, you may be waiting 30+30 minutes or a full hour.

This affects people coming home from bars, staff working at bars, people who start or end a night shift, people going to the airport for an early-morning flight, and people coming from an evening flight that was delayed and didn’t land until midnight or later, and airport workers with early-morning shifts.

So what are the actual problems now? Did Link’s span decrease August 29th? What kinds of trips, where, and when are affected? If in the future ST ends Link even earlier at 10pm or 9 pm every day or on monthly maintenance days or two-week maintenance periods, how big a deal would that be? How would we cope with it? What should we tell Sound Transit and our politicians about all this?

articles.title: Winter Rollback of Pike Place Market Pedestrian Pilot Moves Forward
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Last week, the Pike Place Market Historical Commission gave its unanimous approval to planned adjustments around vehicle access through Seattle's iconic market. Set to be in effect from October through next March, the adjustments represent the newest phase of a pedestrian pilot program that has been in effect for nearly 18 months, but have been lambasted as a retreat on an issue that has widespread city support – restricting unnecessary car traffic through the market.

Under the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) plan , the main corridor along Pike Place will only experience "soft closures" on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays, with the hours vehicles are restricted slightly tightened up to 11am to 4pm. Soft closures mean access is restricted to delivery vehicles, ADA access for disabled patrons, and market vendors.

Apart from major event days when the street will fully close with barricades, through car traffic will be unrestricted along the street with "street closed" signage switched to signage telling drivers to yield to pedestrians.

Pointing to a SDOT survey conducted earlier this year showing 98% support for maintaining vehicle barriers through the Market, a sizable contingent of Seattle urbanists have lamented the move as a backslide that isn't in alignment with the broader city's desires for a more pedestrian-oriented Pike Place. But many Market vendors have argued that they weren't included in the initial launch of the pedestrian pilot in April of 2025, a move made in response to a utility repair project along Stewart Street.

"There are a lot of strong feelings and ideas that we heard from a lot of different people. So, I think ideas are as diverse and dynamic as the number of businesses in the market and all the people who also use this street," Radcliffe Dacanay, the SDOT project manager who has been tasked with leading this work at Pike Place, told commissioners. "There were some increased sales [that] some vendors expressed, but not all vendors experienced increased sales. So, that data is varied. Some sales improved, some vendors [it did] not. But also, just this sense of the Market as a place to come to, and not just an errand space."

The historic commission does get final buy-off on changes of either use or design within the seven-acre historic district. But SDOT's recommendation for the pilot's next phase came about after months of discussions with Market power players, including the commission's chair Jon Cracolici, Alex Hudson from Mayor Katie Wilson's office, members of the Pike Place Merchant's Association (rebooted just this year after being defunct for years), and representatives for the Pike Place Public Development Authority (PDA) which directly maintains operations along the street.

During the meeting, PDA Chief Operating Officer Katie Trent framed the winter access plan as an improvement over last winter, because the PDA had not been enforcing vehicle access restrictions on any weekdays through the Market's quieter months. Trent's comments gloss over the change in signage that will fairly explicitly encourage drivers to head down Pike Place
Trent also provided a new counterpoint to the positive sales data seen at the market in 2025, when it comes to year-over-year (YOY) data for the first half of 2026.

Between January and June, visits to the Market from local residents coming less than 30 miles declined by 11% compared to 2025, a trend that only started to reverse itself in July, with a 1% YOY increase seen in that month. Over those six months, total sales did continue to increase at the Market, but growth slowed from 7% in 2025 to 4.7% this year. Grocery sales took at 4.5% hit during the second quarter, a fact that can likely be traced to the shift in visitor trends during the FIFA Men's World Cup.

"There's all kinds of things that can contribute to what goes on with visitation and sales data, but the street has been an element in there," Trent said. "We have vendors coming to us and saying, 'I'm losing customers because of this, especially in the offseason. Why is the street closed?' That's impactful to what we want to promote as the operator."

The shift toward seasonal operations was bolstered by a study conducted by the University of Washington's Urban Freight Lab – a study that makes some leaps on the way to getting to its conclusions, based on the fact that fewer people visit the Market in the winter overall than in the summer. But it became clear during Wednesday's meeting that SDOT and the PDA had come together to land on a threshold of Market visitation to justify the new schedule: 3,300 Market visitors per hour, or around 55 people passing through the street every minute.
During the summer months, that threshold has been easily met, but in the slower months it has not, according to PDA data from 2025.

Despite presenting the methodology behind the proposal, some merchants and commenters – including members of the advocacy nonprofit group Friends of the Market – wanted to drop soft closures on Fridays. That point of contention pushed this proposal toward looking more like a compromise. It's important to note that the PDA is also empowered to restrict vehicle access if foot traffic is more than expected – and in turn, to cancel soft closures early if the Market is a ghost town on a Friday in February.

"I support this plan. I thought it was very thoughtfully put together. As a vendor, I felt included in the process, both by Urban Freight Lab and the PDA and the working group. I really appreciate what SDOT did in hearing our needs and continues to," Bite Society owner Lendy Hensley said. "I didn't get everything I wanted in this. I suspect no one did, and sometimes I think that is the best kind of agreement. I hope the process continues, as somebody who's looking at Fridays and thinking maybe not that. So I'm hoping for continued conversation as we get to see what these winter months actually look like with this framework in mind."
Plenty of speakers at last week's meeting did provide a voice for the idea of keeping the pedestrian pilot in effect seven days a week.

"I think the thing that I was very disappointed in when I moved to the Market is how uncomfortable it was to shop at the Market and to walk down the streets and try to find my way through the sidewalks," resident Larry Goetz said. "I really appreciate what SDOT did in closing the traffic for the last year and a half, I think it has worked beautifully, especially for the World Cup games. I think it really works. I would like to see it continue."

What happens this winter will likely only set the stage for the Market's next new normal, with SDOT set to return to the commission in January for a proposal for what next summer looks like at Pike Place, without a World Cup to plan around. But at some point, the pilot will need to draw to a close, shifting to a more permanent program.

"I hope that we don't do this every six months," commissioner Mark Childs said ahead of Wednesday's vote. "That this actually builds to something that can last for a period of time, and that there's certainty that people can build around."

articles.title: CHS Pics | ‘ROUND AND ROUND THEY GO’ — Tilted Thunder Roller Derby battles on 15th Ave E
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: There was a taped-out oval on the floor of the Quality Flea Center on 15th Ave E this weekend and it didn’t get there by accident.
Taylor Sloan , who runs the bar at The Hopvine across the street, spent part of her week free-handing a flat track onto the flea market’s concrete floor, no measuring tape required.
“I’ve taped out a million tracks at this point,” Sloan said. “I use upholstery foam and gaffer tape for the pole covers, because it’s supposed to be like a fun, DIY, punk rock sort of thing.”

Sloan has been skating with Tilted Thunder Roller Derby for 17 years. Normally, that means suiting up on the league’s regular turf: a 6,000-square-foot wooden track the team builds from scratch at the fairgrounds in Monroe, home to a growing in popularity event –polished, bleacher-seated, and fiercely competitive. But this weekend at the Quality Flea Center was something else entirely with a stripped-down expo bout, played bank track rules on the flat surface with skaters squaring off against each other for the fun of it.
Sloan also tends bar at the Flea Center whenever it hosts markets and the derby-slash-rock-show idea had been kicking around in her head for a while.
“I wanted to do a crazy, fun, old-school style derby slash rock show, and that’s what this is,” she said. “It’s just an expo bout, just a demo game.”

The music lineup came together the way a lot of good DIY bills do, through a cold DM. Sloan found the band Good Grief on social media and asked them to come play a roller derby show. “They said hell yes,” she said. Daniel Cadaver , a band that’s also played the area, rounds out the bill.

Money-wise, it all came down to ticket sales. “We’ll split with the bands once the cost of the event is covered,” Sloan explained. Unlike Tilted Thunder’s Monroe productions, which come with the overhead of a full fairground buildout, the Quality Flea Center version keeps costs down to the essentials: alcohol insurance, security, and the venue itself. “This is a show,” Sloan said. “I love being very competitive [at the big track], but it’s also fun to take time out of your life to just do something crazy and fun, something that reminds you of another time.”

For anyone on Capitol Hill who’s never seen a bout, Sloan’s pitch is simple: Go find your local league, because there almost certainly is one. Roller derby’s modern era, she said, was built from the ground up by women in the early 2000s, and leagues like Tilted Thunder have been sustaining it ever since on their own time and their own dime. ”
We continue to put all of our time, money, effort, blood, sweat, tears, partners, work, everything, into this sport because it’s just so fun,” Sloan said.
What keeps her coming back, she said, is what makes derby different from a lot of other sports. There’s a role for every body type, and nobody gets left out.
“Every single person, at every single body type, has a purpose and a strength and is celebrated,” Sloan said. “There is no one that is left out or shamed.”
For now, most of the Tilted Thunder action takes places in Monroe but keep your eyes peeled for another visit to the Hill. Learn more at tiltedthunder.org .

articles.title: Plan for higher caps in Broadway Business Improvement Area moves forward
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Watch video of the committee approval here

With the Seattle City Council still in the midst of its summer legislative recess, the city’s lawmakers will have an important piece of Capitol Hill business to addend to when they return to chambers.

Legislation modernizing the assessment structure for the Broadway Business Improvement Area for the first time in over two decades to fund neighborhood clean-up, public safety, and promotion initaitives is planned to come in front of the full council September 15th.

A council committee approved the legislation earlier this month. CHS examined the proposal here. The plan will raise the district’s maximum annual rate from $3,500 to $5,000, expanding its current approximate $200,000 a year budget before adding a recurring $200 annual increase starting in 2032.

During the session, the BBIA’s longtime administrator Egan Orion told the council’s Human Services, Labor, and Economic Development Committee chair Alexis Mercedes Rinck that the change is much needed — and could be the next step in an even more impactful upgrade to the neighborhood clean-up and promotion organization’s finances.

“The costs for garbage pickup and graffiti abatement have increased with inflation, and yet our assessments, especially from our max payers, have remained relatively flat,” Orion told the committee. “So this creates a more equitable assessment for all and it allows the BIA to continue at current service levels plus add back promotion, beautification budgets, event sponsorship, and more.”

Orion said more may be needed and that the BBIA and officials are exploring “a property-based model or establishing a brand-new BIA and sunsetting this particular model”, as property-based assessments “are more sustainable than B&O-based assessments.”

The Broadway BIA was established decades ago as a business-tenant levy. The assessment formula is levied directly on the commercial tenants and operators within the BIA boundary. The typical small-to-midsize business currently pays between $400 and $1,500 annually, depending on its size and reported gross revenue.

A proposed Pike/Pine BIA in the works for years would be property-based. Its formation would give the neighborhood three. The 15th Ave E BIA provides similar services from assessments collected along a core stretch of Capitol Hill’s 15th Ave E.
It is unclear at this point if officials would have the stomach for trying to include the current Broadway BIA zone in a larger IA including Pike/Pine.

A decade ago, the Capitol Hill Chamber of Commerce backed down after a years-long fight against smaller Capitol Hill property owners over a planned expansion of the 1986-born Broadway BIA that would have grown the area to cover most of the Hill including the neighborhoods around Summit/Bellevue, Olive and Denny, Pike/Pine, 12th Ave, 15th Ave, and 19th Ave. The expended energy and flagging membership contributed to the chamber’s shutdown months later .
Some of Broadway’s largest voices are supporting the currently proposed growth for the BIA.

Under the legislation headed for final approval by the full council in September, anchor institutions like Seattle Central College and neighborhood bank branches would become standard maximum-rate payers to reinforce basic maintenance services managed by the BIA across more than 150 businesses along the Broadway commercial corridor.

“We have underpaid for 25 years, and we are probably the largest footprint in the Broadway neighborhood association,” a Seattle Central official said before the August committee vote. “We find it to be absolutely equitable for us to have our limit increased… the value that we receive is massive.”

Committee member, council president, and District 3 representative Joy Hollingsworth did not address the potential larger changes around the Broadway BIA surfaced by Orion but did emphasize the organization’s focus beyond Pike/Pine.

“I think oftentimes North Broadway, the area that you cover, kind of gets left out of the mix,” Hollingsworth said, “because we get so focused on Pike/Pine corridor that we forget that there’s a large part of Capitol Hill that extends to North Broadway and then the area that the BIA covers.”
For now, the Broadway BIA as it stands from E Pike to E Roy is set for a financial boost and any larger changes are being debated outside of City Hall.

articles.title: A Private Investigator Is on the Goose Abuse Case
articles.author: Nathalie Graham
paras: It was a sunny, August afternoon when I called up private investigator Naia Okami. She was hot on the trail of a criminal. I was in need of a scoop.
“The case, as I understand it,” Okami says, “is that somebody essentially beat a Canada goose to death.”

Last week, according to an eyewitness who later posted details of the encounter and pictures of the alleged goose attacker on Reddit, a man took a Canada goose by its neck and slammed it into the concrete sidewalk repeatedly until it was dead. The scene of the crime? Lake Union Park near the Museum of History and Industry. The motive? Unknown. The suspect? Also unknown.

Enter Okami of Cascadia Risk Management. Okami, a trans woman who moved to Seattle during the pandemic, has been an investigator for a variety of firms doing work such as internal corporate investigations and NGO investigations for the past decade. This year, she started her own firm, Cascadia Risk Management, where she employs a mostly trans, entirely queer staff. Though she is no one-trick pony, Okami has specialized in animal crimes throughout her career, both as a volunteer and an investigator. One of her highest profile cases was assisting the Furry Detectives, a group of amateur internet sleuths, in the investigation of Adam Britton, an Australian zoologist and crocodile specialist convicted of sexually abusing dozens of dogs.
When Okami learned of this goose attack, she knew she had to do something.

“It’s the third time somewhat recently this has happened in Seattle,” Okami says. A day after the goose thrashing at South Lake Union, a driver reportedly drove through a family of Canada geese. Just a few years ago, in 2020, a man beat a Canada goose with a cane and then beheaded it in Green Lake.
“This has to stop,” she says. “They’re animals; they’re protected under both federal and state wildlife law. I have the ability to act, so I feel I had the responsibility to act.”

Okami took the case. Her client? Justice. Her payment? Just desserts. Years back, Okami went viral over a clip of her saying, “On all levels except physical, I am a wolf.” For this, and her style, Redditors have called her unserious.

“I’m not your typical gruff ex-cop. I’m early 30s. I dress emo. I listen to emo music. I’m in alt-communities. I don’t look like I do this sort of work, but I do,” Okami says. “I’m passionate about it. I have certifications in it. And I have my own business.”
But the “original wolf girl,” as she brands herself, soon had the scent.

She quickly got a tip after announcing her investigation in the original Reddit thread. Someone knew of this goose killer, but they did not know his name. They sent pictures of him to Okami. She compared those photos to the photos she’d seen of the alleged attacker. Both men had the same tattoos. This was her guy. She reached out to her contact with the fuzz (the Seattle Police Department). Do you know this guy? SPD did not immediately respond to The Stranger ’s request for comment.

Needing more intel, Okami returned to Reddit to search for witnesses and leads. She’s gotten tips, but no official witness statements or affidavits, which are essential to any criminal investigation. If you have something of substance, reach out to Okami to help her get this guy’s goose . Again, no one is paying her for this. This one’s personal.

“I’ve got the skills, I’ve got some free time,” Okami says. “I don’t like living in a city where people hurt the most vulnerable. I don’t like seeing animals and kids get hurt. I’m a trans woman. I come from the south, where people like me get attacked, and I feel like I need to help protect people more vulnerable.”
