articles.title: The Iota at Carrello
articles.author: Meg van Huygen
paras: I will be real with you. I’ve had trouble getting a handle on what Carrello is all about. The sister restaurant to fabulous Altura opened across the street in 2022, and I know the intended bent is Italian-ish, and that chef Nathan Lockwood is a big meat guy who’s finicky about sourcing and breaks down whole animals himself. But what is the concept? I love ending up at Carrello, but the memory of the meal is always slippery. Meaty pasta and beautiful cocktails, no complaints—it’s all a savory, flavory blur. Like, a carrello is a cart. Great, love carts, use them all the time. What exactly is in this cart? There are two things I do always remember about lovely Carrello. One is the dreamy eastern-facing patio and adjacent curated chef’s garden, with all the kaboingy telephone-cord squash tendrils climbing up the fence. And one’s the Iota.

A new friend recently suggested we hit Carrello to try their happy hour menu in its entirety, and I don’t really need to know what kind of cart we’re getting in before accepting this prompt. This is my kind of lady right here. What I didn’t realize is that Carrello’s doing a thing called Abbinamento (Italian for “coupling”) where you can get mini versions of each HH drink and each dish, as a pairing, for $79 total. We let all six drink/snack sets flow all over us, and while it was all a tone poem in hedonism, there were two big standouts. The lamb ribs and peppers are dressed lightly with mint, chili, and toasted rice powder that added a tiny crunch. A mouse stepping on a leaf. You get three small ribs in the mini HH version, stacked like Jenga blocks, with the roasted baby peppers tumbling around them, glistening and winking at you in the candlelight. The rendered lamb fat is so grassy and herby and flavorful, it’s like an umami compound butter all by itself. My word.

And that Iota, which is called the Greek Melon Punch on the HH menu; on the full cocktail list, we learn its true name. Bar director Derek Danley explains that this is a cover of a clarified milk punch. He uses cucumber-infused gin with Acqua di Cedro citrus liqueur, freshly juiced cantaloupe, and Fino sherry infused with four different types of mint from the chef’s garden, along with lemon juice and “our house ferment.” Your what? “Well,” he says, “our kitchen makes this by mixing a ton of seasonal veggies like carrots, celery, onions, and garlic, as well as seasonal stuff like fennel, lovage, radish.” He keeps some of the strained liquid behind the bar to add tang and richness to his cocktails. So Danley takes some that active, funky garden juice, adds all the cocktail’s ingredients to it except the Greek yogurt and milk, and then pours this boozy potion into the dairy mix. “I let that sit for about 30 minutes and then filter everything,” he says. “It’s a process that usually takes about two days to fully filter, but it leaves the cocktail looking crystal clear, while giving it an incredibly luxurious, velvet texture.”

The beverage itself is the palest yellow, made of opalescent sunlight. Not sure why it took society this long to figure out that cantaloupe is the ideal melon for cocktails, not honeydew, but I’m thrilled to live in this era. The aroma of its cousin, the cucumber, hangs in the air over the drink like an enchanted mist, and it’s all imbued with a barely-there minty, milky, citrusy tang. The garden brine is fucking heavenly. With apologies to my nephews, the word that comes to mind is dank . I want to stick my face in the forbidden, ever-changing pickle jar. Put a crazy straw in there that spells out my name. Okay. Now I see. The actual point of Carrello is the garden. This is, I’ve decided, a garden restaurant where they serve various rustic Italian dishes that are accented by the dreamy onsite urban food garden .

After we finish the six-course Abbinamento mini-food/mini-cocktail pairing experience, I order a grown-up Iota for dessert. I want to drink it some more. For this one, Danley serves the drink in a poco grande glass over a custom ice cube, embossed on which seems to be the screensaver maze from my family’s mid-’90s IBM 386. My friend leans in and reveals that she knew I’d love this cocktail and it’s the specific reason she brought me here. I feel known.
I think this is gonna work out. We just get each other now—my new pal and Carrello both.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, August 31–September 6
articles.author: Julianne Bell, Dylan Bueche, Nathalie Graham, Amanda Manitach, Megan Seling, and Nico Swenson
paras: (PERFORMANCE) Jane Don’t is Seattle’s latest star to compete on RuPaul’s Drag Race . If you’ve seen her locally, you already know she was poised to do well. Her drag style uses vintage aesthetics in contemporary ways, combining her knowledge of queer history, fashion references, and her own innovative sewing skills. With a fully glamorous mug, she delivers high-camp performances full of witty pop-culture and classic diva references. Her talents especially come out when she’s handed a microphone to show off her seemingly effortless grasp on comedy. On the show, that skill in particular led her to high praise from comedy giants such as special guest judges Sarah Sherman and Atsuko Okatsuka. If you haven’t gathered yet, she absolutely crushed it, right up until a shocking elimination in the top 5 of Season 18. She made a record-smashing run of high placements, and claimed the title of Miss Congeniality during the finale. Jane Don’t truly made Seattle proud, and proved to the world she is one of the best in the business. She will kick off her extensive Don’t Does America tour in her hometown. ( Emerald City Comedy Club, 7:30, 21+ ) NICO SWENSON
Get yourself some Maui Wowie and snacks and watch 9 to 5

(FILM) Somehow, at the ripe age of 35, I saw 9 to 5 for the first time earlier this year (I know, I know) and couldn’t believe how sharp, funny, joyful, and subversive it was, even today. I have a half-baked conspiracy theory that the streamers bury it on purpose, because what do you mean there’s a scene where Dolly Parton, Jane Fonda, and Lily Tomlin all get zooted on Maui Wowie and indulge in elaborate fantasies of murdering their boss? (Dream blunt rotation for real.) Or that there’s a part where they’re all dressed up in medieval princess costumes ? Not to mention the fact that the film does a much better job of tackling issues like female solidarity, sexual harassment, and sexism in the workplace than a lot of current-day media does, but I digress. In honor of Dolly, I propose this weeknight plan: Pick up some Maui Wowie in your preferred form at your friendly local dispensary, swing by the grocery store for some buttery microwave popcorn and Dolly Parton’s original whipped cheesecake or chocolate pie , and press play on this delightful classic, which is streaming for free on Philo . (Normally I’d recommend you rent it from Scarecrow Video , but that might not be feasible right now, for obvious reasons ). Then read Fonda’s touching tribute to Parton . JULIANNE BELL

(MUSIC) Singer-songwriter, mezzo-soprano, and classically trained pianist Tori Amos needs no introduction. The influential feminist musician’s newest album, In Times of Dragons , tells the story of a woman who transforms into a half-human, half-dragon figure and is described as a “metaphorical story about the fight for Democracy over Tyranny, reflecting the current abhorrent non accidental burning down of democracy in real time by the ‘Dictator believing Lizard Demons’ in their usurpation of America.” Recorded at Amos’s home studio in Cornwall, the album invokes spiritual muses like Teresa of Ávila, the Celtic deity Lugh, and the Egyptian goddess Sekhmet. It also includes characters like a gay witch from Brooklyn and the motorcycling “Gasoline Girls” who “kiss girls”—I’m sold. The Baltimore-based artist/producer Bartees Strange will open. ( Chateau Ste. Michelle, 7 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(VISUAL ART) Becca Fuhrman’s vibrant, color-dense imagery often centers around female protagonists—a celebration of feminine strength, sensuality, and balls. There’s also a thread of the autobiographical peeking out from the nip slips and opulent patterns. In Eat it All , Fuhrman’s first solo Seattle show, the autobiographical punches through as a “rebellious act of survival born from living in the pressure-cooker of beauty culture,” and a protest against the consumerist edict to do anything but grow old. This new body of work is about bodies, our relationship to mortality, and the intensity of being alive. Supple flesh, skulls, a roll of dice, and fallen flowers are traditional vanitas motifs given a fresh spin as they weave throughout paintings and sculptures, like little defiant Easter eggs screaming fuck you to the patriarchy. ( Hometeam Gallery ) AMANDA MANITACH

(MUSIC) With a sound described as “Charli XCX on whippets” and a look modeled on the MySpace-era aesthetic and Y2K bimbo queens, Slayyyter is the bratty, trashy-fabulous diva that the chronically online gays have been waiting for. The “anti-pop star” and former Cookie Monster pajamas girl’s third studio album, WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA , is a no-skips wonder that sounds like it’s been freshly ripped from a hot pink iPod Nano, inspired by her teen years in St. Louis. The lead single “Beat Up Chanel$” evokes, as the lyrics go, “drunk high school nights in parking lots, hanging at the skate park watching the boys, longing for designer items I couldn’t afford,” while “Brittany Murphy” expresses Slayyyter’s suicidal thoughts and her identification with the late Uptown Girls actress. The Showbox stop on her world tour is an opportunity to see an unstoppable artist at the top of her game—plus, a dollar of each ticket sold will be donated to local LGBTQ+ organizations. ( Showbox, 8 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(COMMUNITY) The perfect way to spend a late summer evening is to gather at Green Lake at dusk and learn all about Seattle’s local bat species. Bats Northwest is hosting this informational talk. The length of which depends on the weather and the bats. You can bank on it lasting at least 1.5 hours, though. You will leave as a bat expert. The event is free. But it is a BYOC (bring your own chair) event. ( West Green Lake Beach, 7:15 pm ) NATHALIE GRAHAM

(MUSIC) Phew! Another music festival? But it’s September! Isn’t it time to go back to school and drink hot cocoa under a cozy blanket and pretend to care about football? No! There is still summer fun to be had, as exhausted as you may be, because Bumbershoot is taking over the Seattle Center September 5 and 6 with two days of music, comedy, art, wrestling, fashion, and so much more. (Like, literally there is a mermaid???) We know how overwhelming festivals can be, and this year’s Bumbershoot lineup, while smaller than previous iterations, is still loaded with so much good shit. Bikini Kill! De La Soul! Noname! Peaches! So we did your homework for you and wrote up every! single! band! playing over the weekend, as well as all the fun arts and culture and cat stuff. We crammed it all into an exhaustive guide that you can pick up around town, at the festival, and online at TheStranger.com . Sleep is overrated anyway. ( Seattle Center, times vary, all ages ) MEGAN SELING

(FILM) In French New Wave director Jacques Rivette’s delightful 1974 film Céline and Julie Go Boating , magician Céline (Juliet Berto) and librarian Julie (Dominique Labourier) cross paths in a park in Paris and instantly form a playful bond. Soon, the pair stumbles upon a haunted house that replays a murder-mystery melodrama in an incessant loop, and they become entangled in its repetitive narrative. Rivette worked closely with his two stars to create the film, which ranks at #78 on Sight & Sound ’s list of the 100 Greatest Films of All Time. (Fun fact: It partially inspired the 1985 buddy comedy and Madonna vehicle Desperately Seeking Susan .) At 193 minutes long, this movie isn’t for those with short attention spans, but dreamers will definitely fall under its spell and shouldn’t pass up the chance to see it screened at our film Genius Award winner, the Beacon Cinema. (They’ve also got a bunch of other cool stuff scheduled for this month, including Jess Franco’s 1988 Eyes Without a Face remake Faceless , Charlie Kaufman’s debut Synecdoche, New York , and the Bette Davis melodrama The Little Foxes —check it out!) ( Beacon Cinema, 6 pm ) JULIANNE BELL

Esteemed Italian restaurant Mezzanotte’s end-of-the-summer block party is back for the third year in a row! Take a “Georgetown pause” and come check out this all-time lineup of staff, friends, and locals as Mezzanotte’s garden patio sonically transforms to rival even the sounds of passing planes. For the cost of $20 (a Seattle fiver), there are eight bands—Fan Club, Sux, Ononos, Dish Pit, Scott Yoder, Brat, Microfoam, and Understater—and it starts at 4 p.m. and wraps up around dark (take that, Zoo Tunes), so you can be in bed early Sunday night. All ages are welcome, and kids get in free. ( Mezzanotte, 4 pm, all ages ) DYLAN BUECHE

articles.title: Slog AM: War’s on Again, ICE Detains Man with Stage 4 Cancer, Pike Place Decides to Increase Our Chances of Being Hit By a Car
articles.author: Vivian McCall
paras: War is back: The US and Iran exchanged missiles for the first time since late July. After we claimed to hit two rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz (claiming they were just about to fire missiles carrying naval mines toward the water), Iran struck US bases in Jordan and American military assets in the United Arab Emirates. Iran says our attacks killed and wounded several of its soldiers and civilians. In a feat of verbal hopscotch, the US denies that firing a missile was an act of aggression. It was, of course, a “limited, precise action.”

Speaking of precise: The humanitarian pacifists at Lockheed Martin claim their ballistic missile of the future, the Lockheed Martin Precision Strike Missile, is lethal, long-range and pinpoint. As we have seen since it was first deployed in combat on the first day of our war on Iran, a weapon designed to explode in midair and “propel tens of thousands of dense metal pellets at high speed in all directions” is not pinpoint. Three missiles that struck the city of Lamerd in southern Iran killed civilians 164 feet away from the impact zone.

In apparent defense of the homeland, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents arrested 76-year-old Loreto Javar, a green card holder with Stage 4 prostate cancer during an interview for US Citizenship. He has been detained at the Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma for two months. A retired hotel worker who lives in Fife with his wife and daughter, Javar has no criminal history in the US and has lived here for more than 30 years. In federal court documents, the US government alleges that in the 1970s, Javar spent three years in jail in the Philippines after an “altercation” that left a man dead, the Seattle Times reports .

Authorities claim Javar did not disclose his conviction when he moved to the US to join his father in 1995, which would have made him “inadmissible” at the time. He is “therefore ineligible to remain in the United States now,” ICE said in a statement. Javar’s family and activists want him released. Medical neglect is commonplace in ICE detainment , including untreated cancer. He’s already getting his meals late, which makes it difficult to take his cancer medication on time.

On Friday night, Dolly Parton fans held a candlelit vigil and sing-along to honor their dearly departed queen. “When I heard that Dolly passed, I was just so hungry to be with other people,” vigil organizer Francesca Hays told KUOW’s Casey Martin . “She was the epitome of love and light, and what you want people to be,” said attendee Andrea Leuser, who wore a sparkling, flowing dress and pink butterfly hair clips, “and 80 just wasn’t long enough for a woman like that.”

Five people are dead after a head-on collision 11 miles north of East Wenatchee on State Route 2 late Sunday. Near milepost 137, a westbound Nissan Maxima crossed into the eastbound lanes, slamming head-on into a 2015 Chevrolet Sonic. The male driver of the Nissan and his three male passengers were killed. Two were not wearing seat belts. The driver of the Sonic, a 77-year-old woman, was also killed. The Washington State Patrol says drugs or alcohol were involved.
In South Seattle, a shooting on the 1200 Block of SW Holden Street and Delridge Sunday evening left a 21-year-old in serious condition . The man was taken to Harborview.

One person is dead and 15 are missing after a flash flood at Grand Canyon National Park, reports the Washington Post . At least 62 people were evacuated by air after the flood hit around 2:30 p.m. Sunday afternoon. None of the evacuated were injured. The National Park Service is “seeking information” about hikers, backpackers, and people with camping reservations in affected parts of the canyon a day before the flood.

Walkers, do not rejoice! Last week, the Pike Place Historic Commission unanimously approved the next phase of the pedestrian pilot program, curtailing vehicle access to the market on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays from October through March. If you’re not clued in, this may sound neat, but, it’s the commission bringing back car access five times a week for the first time in 18 months, despite the pedestrian pilot boosting attendance and sales , two things businesses adore. The Urbanist has more .

I know that some of you derive a near-orgasmic pleasure from leaving your Lime bikes and scooters wherever the fuck, but please consider the deafblind people tripping over them . “Safety needs to be number one,” said Mae Lynn Mullen, a Columbia City resident who is deaf and has visual impairment, told the Emerald through a sign language interpreter. “It’s come to a point where [multiple] scooters or bikes are turned over at a four-way intersection, and people are just walking over them and around them. I don’t accept that. We can do better.”
Weather : Mostly sunny with a high of 72. Near perfect. The sky is blindingly blue. The rain may come Tuesday night and it’ll almost certainly be here by Wednesday.

articles.title: Sound Transit Board Greenlights Targeted Fare Gate Retrofits
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: On Thursday, the Sound Transit Board of Directors approved the creation of a fare gate retrofit program set to use $6 million that has been queued up to design a gate pilot at 14 high-ridership Link stations . Those design and planning funds are expected to ultimately turn into an $87 million program that will get gates installed by 2029 or 2030.
Once implemented, the pilot program is expected to recoup costs through higher fare compliance rates within two to three years, according to agency projections.

At last estimate, Sound Transit puts its current light rail fare compliance rate at 63%, based on automatic counters on trains compared to fares paid. The caveat: that figure includes youth under 19, who are not required to pay fares under the state's free youth fare program. Adjusting for free-ride youth would put the compliance rate closer to 70%.

Additionally, Sound Transit's fare ambassador program, which is based on staff members actually checking fares on trains, has measured the fare compliance rate at 85% in 2025, with a further 7.5% of fare-less riders checked being exempt youth. This discrepancy has led some transit advocates to argue the agency is overestimating fare evasion and the potential uptick in fare revenue that gates could prompt.

Sound Transit's financial modeling is based on achieving 95% fare compliance at stations where gates are installed, which staff noted is less that the 98% peer agencies have reported at gated stations. The need to include accessible entry points for people in wheelchairs or with strollers or bikes means the opportunity for fare gate jumping will exist to some extent, although other U.S. transit agencies have estimated that problem as a relatively minor one.

Sound Transit's initial proposal would put bi-directional fare gates at the high-ridership stations in the core of Seattle, Bellevue downtown, and at the ends of lines. Since the gates would be bidirectional and require riders to tap on to enter and tap off to exit stations, staff expect compliance rates to increase systemwide, not just at the gated stations. This is because so many trips end at the stations set to receive gates. With bi-directional gates at key stations, retrofitting all of the system's other stations down the line will likely prove much less lucrative.

"It's important to highlight that while we are showing only boardings at gated and non-gated stations, we're going to need to measure system-wide compliance given the bidirectional nature of the gates, where compliance will be driven both by boardings and alightings," said Brian de Place, Sound Transit's Security and Fare Engagement Executive Director. "And since the vast majority of our riders come in and out of the gated stations, we expect to see compliance levels change at the non-gated stations as well as the gated ones."

About 85% of Sound Transit light rail ridership starts or ends at one of the 14 gates to be targeted for gates, officials said. That traffic has grown rapidly with the extension of the 2 Line across the lake, reaching 160,000 daily riders even before the World Cup came to town.

De Place noted that the agency also opted against trying to quantify the fare compliance benefits at non-gated stations nor the side benefits they hope to achieve – such as lower maintenance costs due to less vandalism – in their financial calculations, although peer agencies, like BART, have reported such benefits after implementing fare gates. If such benefits do come to pass, the financial boost from fare gates could be even larger, he said.

Without factoring in those potential benefits, the agency estimates gates would still boost fare revenue by at least $30 million annually, an increase of more than 30% compared to today's fare revenue across the entire Sound Transit system.

While a nice little boost, that level of revenue is not likely to be large enough to be a major factor in solving the agency's multi-billion-dollar budget gap through 2046. Once estimated at $34.5 billion, the board reduced its long-term budget gap to about $10 billion in May by delaying or tabling a number of expansion projects – and planning to sunset the Sounder N Line commuter rail service. Every little bit helps, though, fare gate supporters have posited.

The fare gate pilot program received a recommendation from the Rider Experience and Operations Committee earlier this month , generating a more in-depth policy discussion at that juncture. King County Councilmember Claudia Balducci noted the agency would need to set its metrics of success for the program, which she painted as a bit squishy so far.

Some boardmembers also raised equity concerns, about potentially making it harder for low-income residents to access the light rail system. King County Executive Girmay Zahilay highlighted those concerns on Thursday, with de Place noting staff was hoping to ramp up participation in the Orca LIFT reduced fare program.

"Brian, just to clarify, you're saying that between now and when fare gates are installed in the next couple of years, we have a specific plan to set up structures or staffing where people can enroll on site for free and reduced fare cards," Zahilay said. "Is that right?"
De Place said yes, with board authorization.

As it stands, staff said about 91,000 people are enrolled in a reduced fare program. Given the Seattle metropolitan area has a population around 4 million, that suggests a fraction of the people eligible are actually enrolled in ORCA Lift or other reduced fare card programs.
In his report to the board on Thursday, Sound Transit CEO Dow Constantine pledged efforts to increase rider awareness as the roll out of the fare gate program approaches.

"Staff have heard loud and clear the emphasis on a thorough and equitable engagement strategy that ensures appropriate fare media and rider awareness materials are available to all passengers once the program is implemented," Constantine said. "Should the board adopt the pilot today, we look forward to keeping you apprised of our progress in tandem with standard design and construction updates you should expect."

After King County Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda raised a question about access for people with disabilities or with bikes in tow, Sound Transit staff assured the board the agency's Request for Proposal would factor in those needs, and that solutions existed.

"As we move into preparing the RFP and actually coming up with the design of these gates, we'll be working really closely with both the ADA community and the bike community in order to understand the specific needs of those communities vis-a-vis gates," said Meg Cederoth, who is deputy chief planning officer at Sound Transit. "And there are multiple systems in the U.S. where the ADA question has been resolved quite comfortably. We'll be making sure we're engaging with our local communities to understand any unique needs here, and then the bike community as well will be working with them to understand that the gates are wide enough."

Another aspect still to be determined is if the fare gates will be rolled out simultaneously at all 14 proposed stations, or on a rolling basis to test the program more incrementally. The board will still need to greenlight the construction funding before the pilot can fully advance.

articles.title: Op-Ed: From the Bargaining Table to Olympia, Educators Need Our Support Now
articles.author: Kelabe Tewolde
paras: It’s the last few weeks of the summer. Everyone is trying to fit in one last trip out of town, hosting cookouts, spending evenings at the lake, or like many parents diving into back to school shopping. Usually educators are gearing up and preparing to welcome back students to the classroom, but this year there is a bit of a road block.

Between now and September 2nd, the first day of school, members of Seattle Education Association (SEA) are bargaining from 9am to 9pm with Seattle Public Schools (SPS) for a fair contract. That was until last night (August 29th), when SPS walked away from the bargaining table as talks broke down regarding cuts to special education.

On August 26th, SEA authorized a strike. This doesn’t necessarily mean they will strike, but SEA’s bargaining team has the greenlight. With the district walking away from the bargaining table it is increasingly likely SEA will have their third strike in 11 years. We are just a few days away from the start of the school year, and you may be asking, “What’s the hold up?”

SEA has agreed to 12 of 57 issues and struggle to find common ground on what holds the most weight in these negotiations, centering the experience of their students and members. They have found that pressurization and wages are where the district and SEA are unable to come to an agreement. You may be wondering, what this actually means. Teachers are focused on pressurization, a.k.a. increased workload. Pressurization comes in the forms of increases in caseload, class size, and other demands that take their time and focus away from students and lead to educator burnout.

When we constantly put more and more on our educators' plates, we limit the time and energy they have to actually teach our children. And when we talk about wages, we mean making sure all SPS employees can afford to live in the city where they work. In a city as expensive as Seattle, many of the lower-paid workers are finding it difficult to afford to live here in the communities they serve. Educators are not looking for a massive raise in this contract. It is simply a cost-of-living adjustment that will ease the burden of affordability.
If I were to simplify that for the everyday person not at the bargaining table: Teachers want to improve working conditions because their working conditions are their students' learning conditions.
SEA is digging into the district’s annual $1.3 billion budget and finding that part of the problem is state funding. And part of the problem is misplaced priorities.
What is SEA fighting for beyond pressurization and wages?

Special education students have a civil right to a high-quality education : That means we need to meet their individual education plan (IEP). With more students with IEPs in general education, SPS needs to ensure that the co-teaching models are effective. Teachers need an opportunity and space in their schedule to collaborate and help ALL of their students succeed. In these co-teaching models, SPS needs to have a plan to fill in for vacancies and leaves so students with IEPs have teachers with a Special Education endorsement. This is not only an issue around providing a high quality education for all our students, but it is a civil rights issue.

Reasonable class sizes: This is critical to how students succeed. Currently, SEA’s contract includes overage pay as an incentive for the district to keep class sizes a reasonable size, but we are hearing from educators that they don’t want that overage pay. On a personal note, my friend that teaches in a different district similarly had overage pay for having a large class. Mid-year, she had to advocate to split the class up because the learning environment in a class of 35 students was not conducive to student success.

Smaller class sizes give educators the ability to connect with students and help them succeed. SEA states: “We need to create a true cap, beyond which the district must add staff or reduce the class size to ensure students have the opportunity to learn.”
Beyond class sizes, SEA has a variety of other proposals that include safety, AI usage in the classroom, and substitute reimbursement.
Long term, we need solutions from the state
These issues could be solved at the state level if we had a legislature that would prioritize the learning conditions of our children.

In 2014, we had the opportunity to implement smaller class sizes through I-1351 , providing students with one-on-one attention from caring and qualified teachers and support staff. While voters backed smaller class sizes, the state legislature unfortunately left the initiative unfunded, and in 2015 the state legislature delayed its implementation. Eventually in 2017, the legislature repealed the cap on class sizes, due to a lack of funding, leading us to the mess we are in now: Large class sizes, teachers without the resources to effectively serve their students, and students failed by a system that they simply inherited.

Teachers are burnt out and it reflects in how many educators are leaving our schools. One special education teacher told me that: “Last year was the worst teacher year of my life due to an unsustainable and unsupported SpEd caseload. And every SpEd teacher in my building except one left at the end of last year. It’s leading to massive burnout and attrition.”
Without proper class sizes and support, we are failing our teachers, and in turn failing our children.
Many critics to this solution will bring up, “if smaller class sizes were unfunded in 2014, how would you fund them now, especially with an upcoming austerity budget?”

Well, simply put, we would need to reform our tax code like WEA recommended about a decade ago. I’m writing this off the heels of Washington State coming in as No. 1 — for corporate tax breaks and corporations like Microsoft paying a tax rate of 2.4%, while people that earn less than $33,500 a year have a tax rate of 13.8% . We need a legislature that is bold enough to stand up for our values and provide a quality education for all, while creating a sensible tax code that makes everyone pay their fair share .

And this November, we have a choice in legislative races all over the state. We need to elect legislators that are willing to balance the tax code. We deserve legislators who will stand with workers over corporate profits. And legislators that support our educators all year long, not just during an election year.

In the upcoming days, I ask you to support our teachers. This could be showing up for the bargaining team at rallies, spreading the word via social media, calling on the district to meet SEA’s proposals , and, if there is a strike, picketing with teachers throughout the city demanding SPS meet their proposals.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Washington’s Primary Election Results Underscore the Case for Proportional Ranked Choice Voting
articles.author: Zane Gustafson
paras: From Seattle to Spokane and everywhere in between, August’s primary results show an electorate yearning for more options, and proportional ranked choice voting is the way to make viable candidates from outside the two-party system.

Contrary to the blinkered two-party analysis in the Seattle Times , which explicitly excluded independent candidates and ignored major differences between Democrats, Washington primary voters showed they support three viable statewide political parties: Democrats (40% of the statewide Congressional primary vote), Republicans (35%), and an emerging left-wing party (20%).

For this analysis, I analyzed candidate websites for rhetoric and policy platforms to identify which candidates are running as establishment or moderate Democrats and which candidates are running on progressive or socialist platforms. The left-wing label includes members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) like State Rep. Shaun Scott, progressive Democrats like Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal, Brent Hennrich, and Kevin Fagan, and independent left-wing candidates like Kshama Sawant and Melissa Chaudhry.

These primary results are evidence of what is already known in Olympia: that the governing Democratic Party in Washington State is a coalition of at least two smaller parties. Or, as Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen put it on my podcast Ungerrymander America : “I’m already the leader of a multiparty coalition called the Democratic Party, that includes a broad range of people. From people who, if you could just get them to say what they think, identify as communists or socialists, to people who in a different time could easily have been Republicans, and everything in between.”

Though this emerging left-wing party is not yet formalized, candidates espousing anti-establishment, progressive, or socialist rhetoric and policies are finding support across the state. In addition to former Congressional Progressive Caucus chair Pramila Jayapal (WA-7), left-wing candidates received enough votes across Western Washington to prevent four incumbent Democratic Congresspeople from reaching 50% of the vote: Rick Larsen (WA-2), Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (WA-3), Adam Smith (WA-9), and Marilyn Strickland (WA-10).

Across the mountains in Eastern Washington's Fifth Congressional District, incumbent Republican Michael Baumgartner underperformed, receiving just 47.4% of the vote. The remaining 52.6% was split between mainstream Democrats, progressives, and independents.

Failing to win 50% of the vote means Baumgartner is vulnerable. But for challenger Carmela Conroy to win, she will need to build a cross-spectrum coalition that includes everyone from the 4.4% of voters who voted for left-wing candidates to the more than 20% of voters who voted independent. Conroy's coalition building efforts were helped by the full-throated endorsement of her by independent Nate Powell, who finished third with 16.5% of the primary vote.
Taken together, over one-quarter of primary voters voted for either a left-wing or independent alternative to the two-party system to represent them in Congress.
The same kind of multiparty dynamic is playing out in legislative races across Washington State.

First, contests in the 37th and 43rd districts show that Seattle has a two-party system of moderate/establishment Democrats being challenged by progressive Democrats and DSA-candidates. Both districts will send a DSA-member to the legislature, with the 43rd's Shaun Scott running unopposed for reelection and the 37th’s Jaelynn Scott winning an overwhelming 88% of the primary vote.

Both districts have contested races, with the establishment Democrat Sen. Jamie Pedersen favored to win reelection in the 43rd. On the other hand, left-wing challenger Kelabe Tewolde won more than 51% in the primary in the 37th. These results should not be interpreted as definitive victories for either the moderates or the progressives; the key takeaway is that there are two distinct factions competing across Seattle districts and the more left-leaning democratic socialist faction is making headway and establishing itself as a distinct political force.

This isn’t only playing out in Seattle. Left-wing candidates are making gains elsewhere too. In the redrawn 14 th district that stretches from Yakima to the Tri-Cities, incumbent Republican Rep. Deb Manjarrez received 51% of the primary vote, showing that the district will be competitive in November. In the race for second place, the labor and immigrant rights activist Ezequiel Morfin beat self-described moderate Tony G. Sandoval. To be clear, Morfin identifies as a Democrat. I categorize him as part of this emerging left-wing party because his platform centers working families and places his campaign in opposition to corporate donors and party insiders.

Meanwhile, voters in Eastern Washington are looking for independent alternatives. In addition to Nate Powell coming within 3% of second place in the Fifth Congressional District, the 6th Legislative District had independent Aaron Croft come within 259 votes of advancing to the general. Powell and Croft were two of five independent candidates in Eastern Washington endorsed by the Independent Veterans of America .

The concurrent and separate races for the two State House seats in the 6th LD show the appeal of independents. For seat #1, four Republicans combined for 57% of the vote while two Democrats received 42%. But just 50% of 6th LD voters supported Republican Jonathan Bingle for seat #2. Some 2,000 voters, 7% of the 6th LD primary electorate, voted Republican in one race then voted Independent in the other.

Take it all together and the shape of Washington’s multiparty politics comes into focus: the governing moderate to center-left Democrats fighting off a challenge from a left-wing party currently strong in Seattle and growing across the state; and a Republican Party losing relevancy in the State Legislature facing challenges from increasingly organized independent candidates.

Unfortunately, the structure of Washington’s top-two voting system is artificially keeping the two-party system in place and contributing to the widespread political cynicism that contributes to many people opting-out of voting. Voter turnout in the 2026 primary was just 37%, lower than the more than 40% turnout in midterm primaries in 2022 and 2018.

By implementing a proportional voting system, such as proportional ranked choice voting (RCV), Washington could send a multiparty delegation to Congress and have a formal multiparty politics in the State Legislature. This would help heal our political cynicism by providing voters real options beyond the two-party system.

Instead of a winner-take-all system like we have now, where the candidate with 50.1% of the vote wins and the other 49.9% of the district is left without, proportional RCV elects multiple winners in the same district. This means far more than 50% of voters will see someone they voted for win the election. For example, in a district where the top three candidates win, 75% of voters would be represented; in a four-winner district this goes up to 80%.

Individual candidates would still need to win at least 20% of the vote to be elected in a four-winner district. For a deep dive on the mechanics, see chapter 6 of my 2024 book Polemic for Democracy on the Ungerrymander America blog .
Finally, if implemented, the multiple winner function of proportional RCV makes gerrymandering functionally impossible , according to analysis by the Brennan Center for Justice.

Shifting to proportional RCV for electing members of the State House could be done through the normal legislative process, while changing the voting system for the Senate may require amending the state constitution ( Article 2, Section 6 ).

But, such a change may be unlikely to be popular among legislators bought into the existing two-party system. A final option if legislation for proportional RCV fails to gain traction in Olympia would be for Washington voters to bring an initiative to demand a better voting system that would give them more options.

The primary results show that at least 25% of voters are already putting their votes toward alternatives to the two-party status quo. And if there were a real chance to change the system? Who knows how broad the support for such an initiative might reach.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more. Every place on the list has been open for at least six months, proving its merit.

Like many menus, this map updates every quarter — removal from the Eater 38 doesn’t mean a restaurant isn’t still awesome and won’t return in the future. articles.title: Seattle Transit Trivia Answers
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Thank you to everyone to joined Seattle Transit Trivia on Monday. After a competitive game, top scores are:

If you are one of top scorers, please check your email for information about the prizes. This post will share the correct answers for all 39 questions. If you missed the game on Monday but want to test your Seattle transit knowledge, check out the questions from Round 1 , Round 2 , and Round 3 .
Q1: How many transit agencies support ORCA cards?

Nine: Community Transit, Everett Transit, King County Metro, Kitsap Transit, Pierce Transit, Sound Transit, Washington State Ferries, Seattle Center Monorail, Seattle Streetcar. RandomNerd answered correctly first .
Q2: What was the first bus rapid transit line operated by an ORCA agency?
The Swift Blue Line opened in 2009. Henry Horenstein answered correctly first .
Q3: Which bus route(s) operated by an ORCA agency do not connect with any other bus routes from the same agency?
Pierce Transit Route 497 is isolated from the rest of the PT bus network. The route is a peak only service between Landland Hills and Auburn station. Henry Horenstein answered correctly first .
Q4: Which Sound Transit route has stops outside the Sound Transit taxing district?
Sound Transit Route 595 serves stops in Gig Harbor. Aaron Gu answered correctly first .
Q5: List each King County Metro route that is branded as an express service.
Metro’s once expansive network of express bus routes has dwindled down to just 5 routes: 9X, 17X, 21X, 28X, 193X. Aaron Gu answered correctly first .
Q6: One King County Metro RapidRide bus has a rear window. Which bus?
Bus 6000 has a rear window. This vehicle usually operates on the A Line or F Line. HZ answered correctly first .
Q7: Which Community Transit Express route does not stop at a Link station?
CT Express Route 907 travels between Paine Field and Stanwood. All other Express routes stop at a Link station. HZ answered correctly first .
Q8: When did the oldest transit vehicle still used on scheduled routes by an ORCA agency enter service?
The Carlisle II began passenger service on April 9, 1917. The boat is still used on the Port Orchard ferry route more than 100 years later. Senior answered correctly first .
Q9: Rank the following transit agencies from highest to lowest based on their June 2026 ferry/water taxi ridership: King County Metro, Kitsap Transit, Washington State Ferries.
WSF had 1,956,901 passengers, Kitsap Tranit had 127,204 passengers, and the Metro Water Taxi had 86,707 passengers. Aaron Gu answered correctly first .
Q10: How many ORCA card taps were recorded in 2025?
ORCA recorded 76,671,844 taps in 2025. Aaron Gu answered correctly first .
Q11: What was the first ferry route operated by the Washington State Department of Transportation (or one of its predecessors)?
Washington state began operating the Keller Ferry in 1930, 21 years before Washington State Ferries took over ferry routes in Puget Sound. Henry Horenstein answered correctly first .
Q12: In Fall 2025, how many average daily boardings did the busiest Metro bus stop have across all routes?

The Metro stop at 3rd & Pike (northbound) had an average of 2,950 boardings each day . The stop is served by routes 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 13, 14, 36, 70, 125, C Line, D Line, and E Line. Aaron Gu answered correctly first .
Q13: Which Link station is shown in the picture below?
The vertical concrete slats are a unique feature to Symphony station. Aaron Gu answered correctly first .
Q1: Which route operated the last scheduled bus trip through the Downtown Seattle Transit Tunnel?
Route 41 ran the last scheduled trip in the DSTT just after midnight on March 23, 2019. Henry Horenstein answered correctly first .
Q2: How many boardings did Everett Transit record on its free shuttles on July 4, 2026?

The free Everett Transit shuttles carried an incredible 10,192 passengers on July 4. To put that into perspective, the rest of the Everett Transit network had about 2,500 trips on the same day. Henry Horenstein answered closest without going over.
Q3: Rank the following jurisdictions from most to least based on the number of number of bus stops used by King County Metro in Fall 2025: Bothell, Issaquah, Kent, Redmond, Renton, Shoreline
The correct order is: Kent (306 stops), Renton (295 stops), Redmond (234 stops), Shoreline (222 stops), Bothell (79 stops), Issaquah (77 stops). No one got this completely correct.
Q4: Excluding Trailhead Direct, shuttle routes, and school routes, which King County Metro bus routes with at least one stop in Seattle have zero stops within 1000ft of a Link station?
Only three routes meet this criteria: Route 22 and DART routes 773, 775. Blumdrew answered correctly first .
Q5: The first double decker bus in Puget Sound entered service on August 1, 2007. What route did it first operate?
Community Transit rolled out their first double decker bus on Route 402. Scooby Doo and the Goblin King answered correctly first .
Q6: Identify one location (Link station and direction) in Seattle where Link shuttle buses use a stop not shared by any other routes.
Southbound Link shuttles at Rainier Beach station use a dedicated stop. Scooby Doo and the Goblin King answered correctly first .
